extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of medieval/early-modern Italian history and comparative civic governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and institutional requirements from a historical narrative about Pistoia and Cremona (podestà selection, factional conflict, and remedies used by rulers). Useful for understanding what the author treats as desiderata for stable city government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podestà eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The podestà should be a foreigner and a citizen of another city, agreeable to the council, not related by blood to any of the electors, possess real estate in the city or country, and have attained at least thirty-six years of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states this rule arose to avoid contests among principal families; upon election they were sent letters praying them to accept, and on entry were solemnly received with public concourse and acclamations. (Original wording: 'it was now ordained by law, that none should be elected to the office of podesta who was not a foreigner... had a real estate... and was arrived at least to thirty-six years of age.' )

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer men of prudence and established reputation for magistracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors sought 'men of prudence and eminent reputation' for office, particularly for the podestà.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes choosing individuals of moderation and spirit to remedy disorders; such persons were expected to be above factional interests. This is given as a preventive measure against internal contests and seditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podestà must have military talent and legal competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Podestàs were generally men 'of military talents, as well as skilful in the laws' and they brought judges expert in legal science to hear civil and criminal causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation: the podestà should be capable both of military leadership and of judicial-administrative governance; they 'conducted with them judges expert in the legal science, by whose means they heard and tried all causes civil and criminal, and assembled the council when it was necessary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial and institutional trappings of office
rubrics_metrics.description: On entry the podestà carried insignia of authority (furred cap, long sword, rod, and sceptre) and were publicly received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremony served to legitimize authority and signal the office-holder's role and dignity; the text details public concourse, acclamations, and the carrying of emblems to mark legitimate rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary suspension and centralization of municipal offices in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of severe disorder the duke suppressed existing magistracies and offices and consigned administration of revenues and charities to appointed proveditors or commissaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the duke 'elected four commissaries for the affairs of Pistoia' and appointed 'Proveditors General' who received the moveables of the public palace; six citizens were deputed Proveditors of the Commons. This is presented as an explicit remedy to restore order when local magistracies fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limited military force to disarm sedition and secure tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign may send a modest force to disarm citizens, restrain the seditious, and amplify defenses to rein in disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the duke sent 350 soldiers to disarm the citizens and reinforce fortifications. Guidance implies measured, targeted use of force to restore governance rather than wholesale repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore public honours/offices to revive population, commerce, and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Deprivation of honours and offices can lead to depopulation, diminished commerce and revenue; restoring them is necessary to return the city to its primitive state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Cosimo restoring honours and privileges (in 1547) because their removal reduced population and economic activity; the author frames this as a corrective policy to reverse decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary punishment to deter future disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Public and exemplary punishment of offenders can intimidate followers and restore public tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the duke 'punished the prisoners in an exemplary manner' after masked processions that risked reviving ancient animosities; the author presents such penalties as a tool to secure long-term peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid factional division; ensure constitutional balances
rubrics_metrics.description: Disunion of citizens and dominance by a few families leads to perpetual factional warfare; a good constitution with an independent executive, multiple legislative branches, and an independent judiciary is necessary to prevent oligarchic domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that without an 'independent executive power, three independent branches in the legislature, and an independent judicial department' prominent families will divide a state into parties that 'tear one another to pieces.' This is offered as a structural remedy rather than reliance on individual virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public works and administrative competence affect civic stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Poorly executed public works (e.g., water conduit) provoke popular complaints and can rekindle demands for changes in government form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Muraiur conduit produced such complaints that the people rose in tumults and insisted on choosing a podestà. The implicit lesson: competent provision of public utilities is a governance responsibility that, if neglected, fuels instability.
